✻ Cogitated for 54s · done Wednesday 8:40 PM

※ recap: Goal: build the Mize reservations ingest API with dedup and per-supplier throttling, step by step, with tests. Steps 1 to 3 are done and all 76 tests pass; next is Step 4, the sliding window log rate limiter, when you say go.

> explain why we had to make costume SqlMappers, what problem did it solve?     

● Short version: SQLite has no date or decimal type, so we had to decide how to
  store them. The custom mappers make that decision once, in one place, and make
  sure Dapper uses it for both writing and reading. That matters because dedup
  depends on a value reading back exactly as it was written.

  The underlying problem

  SQLite has five storage types: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT and BLOB. There is no
  DateTimeOffset and no decimal. Whatever we store has to be converted on the
  way in and out, and the defaults weren't good enough.

  What went wrong without the mappers

  Dates (observed). Before I added the handler workaround, the scratch test
  showed that a DateTimeOffset was written as 2026-08-01 00:00:00+00:00. That is
  Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's native format, and it keeps whatever offset the value
  had. That causes two problems:
  - The same instant sent as 02:00+02:00 and as 00:00Z would be stored as
    different text. That's untidy to debug and not reliably sortable or
    comparable as text.
  - The format isn't fixed-width and isn't under our control, so we'd depend on
    a library detail.

  Decimals (less clear-cut). SQLite's REAL type is a binary float, so a REAL
  column would turn 450.10 into something like 450.1000000001. That would break
  SameDetailsAs. I believe Microsoft.Data.Sqlite already writes decimals as text
  by default, so the decimal handler is mostly insurance. It guarantees
  invariant formatting with no culture surprises (450,10 under de-DE) and
  preserves the scale (450.00). I haven't tested what happens without it, so I
  can't claim it fixed a failure I saw. The date handler is the one that
  definitely mattered.

  Why this matters for dedup

  The whole feature rests on one comparison: does the stored reservation equal
  the incoming one? If a value changes slightly on the round trip (a different
  offset, lost precision, float drift), an identical resend looks different. It
  would be reported as Updated instead of Duplicate, and a pointless write would
  happen. The handlers pin the format down (UTC, fixed width, 7 digits of tick
  precision, invariant culture), and the unit tests lock it in.

  Why a workaround was needed (RemoveTypeMap)

  Dapper already knows DateTimeOffset and decimal as built-in types. For those,
  it uses its own mapping when writing parameters and never calls a custom
  handler's SetValue. So AddTypeHandler alone would have appeared to work for
  reading while silently being ignored for writing. Removing the built-in
  mapping first makes Dapper use ours for both directions.

  Costs

  - Dapper's handler registry is global to the process. I guard it so it runs
    only once, but it is hidden global state.
  - RemoveTypeMap is a non-obvious step, which is why DapperConfiguration and
    CLAUDE.md both explain it.
  - The alternative was to convert explicitly in the repository (the converter I
    briefly had). That has no global state, but it spreads conversion code
    through the repositories. You asked for handlers, and with handlers Dapper
    can map rows straight into the records, which makes the repositories
    shorter.

  I haven't changed anything. Say "go" when you want Step 4.

● The decimal handler turned out to be half necessary, so I removed the half
  that wasn't. All 72 tests pass, down from 76. I deleted the scratch test
  afterward.

  What the experiments showed
  - No decimal handler at all: every case failed. The Price column is TEXT, so
    Dapper can't map it into the record's decimal constructor parameter. The
    reading side is required.
  - Handler for reading only, no RemoveTypeMap: all 6 cases passed under de-DE.
    They were 450.10, 450.00, 0.1, 0, decimal.MaxValue and the smallest positive
    decimal. Duplicate detection held for each. Microsoft.Data.Sqlite already
    writes decimals as invariant text, so the custom write path added nothing.

  What I changed
  - DecimalTypeHandler:
    - It's now read-only. Parse accepts stored text, and anything that isn't
      text throws.
    - I removed the numeric-input branch, because a TEXT column can't produce
      one.
    - SetValue stays only because Dapper's base class requires it. It's never
      called, and the comment says so.
  - DapperConfiguration:
    - I removed the RemoveTypeMap calls for decimal.
    - DateTimeOffset keeps its RemoveTypeMap, because it needs the handler for
      both directions.
    - Comments explain why the two types differ.
  - Tests:
    - I deleted the write-side decimal tests, since they tested code that never
      runs.
    - The new ones cover exact parsing of stored text (including
      Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's own forms like 450.1 and ...335.0), culture
      invariance, no float drift, and malformed or non-text input.
  - Docs: CLAUDE.md and the plan now say the decimal handler is read-only and
    why.

  One small trade-off: stored prices now look like 450.1 instead of 450.10. The
  numeric value is identical and comparison ignores scale, but if you ever read
  the database by eye, that's why. Microsoft.Data.Sqlite owns that text format.
  The reader accepts any invariant decimal text, so a future format change
  wouldn't break it.

  I haven't started Step 4. Say "go" when you want it.

● Step 4, the rate limiter, is done and I stopped before Step 5. A full rebuild
  gives 0 warnings and 0 errors, and all 113 tests pass (84 before, 29 new). I
  didn't touch git.

  What was built (RateLimiting/)
  - SlidingWindowRateLimiter:
    - It implements the sliding window log you asked for. Each supplier has a
      log of the timestamps of its permitted requests, in a
      ConcurrentDictionary. It's a singleton, with a lock per supplier.
    - A request is permitted if fewer than 100 logged requests are younger than
      60 seconds. A rejected request is not logged, so the window clears as the
      spec says.
    - It returns RetryAfter, the time until the oldest logged request leaves the
      window, which Step 6 will use for the Retry-After header.
  - ISupplierRateLimiter, RateLimitResult, RateLimitOptions:
    - The options default to 100 requests per 60 seconds and are bound from a
      RateLimiting section I added to appsettings.json.
    - Supplier ids are matched exactly, so case matters.
  - RateLimitOptionsValidator: a non-positive limit or window is rejected.
  - AddSupplierRateLimiting(): the DI registration, called from Program.cs.

  Two choices beyond the plan
  - The log stores monotonic timestamps from TimeProvider.GetTimestamp(), not
    wall-clock times. A clock adjustment on the server can't shorten or stretch
    the window. The clock is read inside the lock, so the log stays in order
    when requests arrive at once.
  - Options are validated at startup. I confirmed this with a real run. With
    PermitLimit=0 the app refuses to start with PermitLimit must be greater than
    zero., and with the defaults it starts normally.

  Tests
  - Behavior:
    - The first 100 requests are permitted and the 101st is rejected.
    - RetryAfter shrinks as time passes.
    - A request exactly one window old has expired.
    - The window is truly rolling: 50 requests at t=0 and 50 at t=30 expire
      independently.
    - A burst straddling a boundary can't double the limit.
    - Rejected requests don't extend the window.
    - Suppliers are isolated, ids are case-sensitive, and blank ids throw.
  - Concurrency: 300 parallel requests give exactly 100 permitted. Across 10
    suppliers at once, each gets exactly 100.
  - Config and wiring: defaults, config overrides, invalid config, singleton
    lifetime, and TimeProvider handling.
  - The tests can fail. I deliberately introduced three bugs, and the suite went
    red for each:
    - counting rejected requests failed 2 tests;
    - an off-by-one at the window boundary failed 5;
    - removing the lock failed both concurrency tests.
    - I restored the code afterward and confirmed no trace of the bugs remains.

  Known limitation for the README: limiter state lives in memory, so it resets
  on restart and isn't shared between instances. Production would need external
  storage such as Redis. Idle suppliers' logs are also never evicted, which is
  fine at this scale. The id length limit (#6) from the earlier review is still
  open, to be done in Step 6.

  I also updated the plan and CLAUDE.md. Say "go" for Step 5, the ingestion
  service.

  Why it was coupled to supplierId

  It wasn't really. SlidingWindowRateLimiter always keyed a dictionary on a
  plain string, and only the names and doc comments said "supplier". I wrote it
  for the one use case in front of me, which is a naming habit and not a design

    passes the supplierId as the id. I left the Step 5 line as it was, because
    that is where the app supplies the supplier id.

  Validation attributes versus IValidateOptions

  Both are standard. They suit different jobs:

  ┌─────────┬────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │         │  Validation attributes ([Range]    │   IValidateOptions<T>    │
  │         │  plus ValidateDataAnnotations())   │        (current)         │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ Best    │                                    │ rules across properties, │
  │ for     │ simple rules on a single property  │  or rules that need      │
  │         │                                    │ injected services        │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ Code    │ declarative and short, with no     │ a validator class plus a │
  │         │ extra class or registration        │  registration            │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │         │ TimeSpan ranges are awkward:       │                          │
  │ Weak    │ [Range(typeof(TimeSpan),           │ more code for simple     │
  │ spot    │ "00:00:00.0000001",                │ rules                    │
  │         │ "365.00:00:00")]                   │                          │
  ├─────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ Testing │ needs a Validator call or a DI     │ plain unit tests, as I   │
  │         │ container                          │ have now                 │
  └─────────┴────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

  My view is that attributes are the more idiomatic default when every rule is
  independent and per-property, as they are here: PermitLimit > 0 and Window > 
  0. The TimeSpan range string is the main cost. IValidateOptions is the better
  tool as soon as rules depend on each other, for example "window must exceed X
  when the limit is above Y". That isn't the case today.

  So the current validator is defensible but slightly heavy for two plain rules.
  Switching would remove one class, one registration and one test file's worth
  of code, and I'd keep the tests by validating through the Validator. I haven't
  changed it, because you asked which is better practice, not for a change.

  Do you want me to switch to attributes, or keep the validator? Otherwise say
  "go" for Step 5, the ingestion service.

> why did you use _gate for the locking? is it common practice?                 

● Yes, a dedicated private object to lock on is the standard practice. The name
  _gate is just my naming choice.

  Why a separate lock object

  The usual rule, from Microsoft's guidance and common .NET style, is to lock on
  a private object that nothing else can reach. Locking on anything shared has
  pitfalls:
  - lock (this) lets any caller who holds a reference to the object take the
    same lock. That can cause deadlocks you can't see from inside the class.
  - lock (typeof(X)), or locking on a string, is shared across the whole
    process, so unrelated code can collide on it.
  - Locking on the data structure itself, here the Queue<long>, would work,
    since the queue is private. But a dedicated object states the intent, and
    the lock keeps working if someone later swaps the queue for something else.

  Why the lock is per supplier and not global

  The lock lives inside each RequestLog, so two different ids never wait on each
  other. A single global lock would serialize every request in the app for no
  reason.

  Why not a thread-safe collection or SemaphoreSlim
  - ConcurrentQueue doesn't help. Each operation is thread-safe on its own, but
    the limiter needs a check-then-act sequence that must be atomic: drop
    expired entries, check the count, then add. Separate thread-safe calls don't
    combine into one atomic step, and two threads could both see 99 and both
    add.
  - SemaphoreSlim suits async code. You can't await inside a lock, but there is
    nothing to await here. The critical section is a few queue operations and
    never blocks on I/O. A plain lock is cheaper and simpler.

  On the name

  _gate is fine and I've seen _syncRoot and _sync too, but _lock is probably the
  most common convention. .NET 9 also added a dedicated System.Threading.Lock
  type, which this project (on .NET 8) can't use yet. Renaming to _lock is
  trivial if you prefer it, and I haven't changed anything.

  Say "go" for Step 5, the ingestion service.

✻ Cogitated for 10s · done 8:25 AM

> do you think its better to stay with the _gate or lock on the queue?          

● I'd stay with the dedicated object. Both are correct here, though, so the
  difference is small.

  Why the dedicated object wins
  - Intent is explicit. A field named for locking says that this is the
    synchronization point. lock (_timestamps) makes a reader work out whether
    the queue is also being used as a lock deliberately or by accident.
  - It survives refactoring. If the queue is ever replaced, wrapped, recreated,
    or handed to another method, a lock on it silently changes meaning. Locking
    on a reassigned field is a classic bug. A separate readonly object never
    changes.
  - It matches the convention. Reviewers recognize private readonly object _lock
    immediately. Locking on the collection also invites the "who else touches
    this?" question, which is the question the dedicated object avoids.

  The cost is negligible. One small object per supplier, and each supplier's log
  already holds a queue of up to 100 numbers.

  Where locking on the queue would be fine. For a private, never-reassigned
  field that nothing else touches, it's safe and arguably less code. That is
  true of _timestamps today. The saving is one line, which isn't worth losing
  the clarity.

  If you want to align with convention, I'd rename _gate to _lock, since that is
  the more common name. It's a pure rename. I haven't changed anything. Say
  "go" for Step 5, the ingestion service.

› Message from general-purpose
  ## (a) Verdict
  Step 4 is correct and conforms to the spec. The 101st request is the first
  rejected, only permitted requests are logged, and the window clears. I found
  no bugs. The design is compact, well documented and well tested for an
  interview assignment. The remaining issues are minor, and a few are things to
  handle deliberately in Steps 5-7.

  ## (b) Findings

  **Verified correct (no action needed)**
  - **Boundary (SlidingWindowRateLimiter.cs:48).** `elapsed >= window` dequeues,
  so a request exactly one window old counts as expired. `Count >= permitLimit`
  (:53) rejects the 101st and permits the 100th.
  - **RetryAfter (:56).** It is always strictly positive. After the dequeue
  loop, the peeked timestamp has `GetElapsedTime(...) < window`, computed by the
  same function and the same `now`, so `window - elapsed > 0` even if
  `TimeProvider.System`'s double-based tick conversion truncates. At most it is
  off by sub-tick rounding. It is accurate: it equals the time until the oldest
  counted request leaves.
  - **Atomicity.** The clock read, prune, check and enqueue all sit inside one
  per-key `lock` (:43-62). The queue stays chronological, and `Queue<long>` is
  never touched outside the lock.
  - **GetOrAdd (:31).** The static lambda is fine. A racing duplicate
  `WindowLog` is discarded harmlessly and never observed.
  - **Overflow and extreme values.** `GetElapsedTime` uses long subtraction and
  double math, so there is no practical overflow with the one-day cap. A very
  large `PermitLimit` is harmless because the queue grows lazily with actual
  permitted requests.
  - **Config binding.** Binding of init-only properties works (the DI test
  proves it).
  - **Culture.** The Range string bounds are culture-safe (the test covers
  de/fr/th).

  **Should-fix / worth deciding**
  1. **Whitespace ids throw (SlidingWindowRateLimiter.cs:29).**
     - `ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace` throws `ArgumentException`. A supplierId of `"
  "` that slips past validation would surface as a 500.
     - Validate-then-throttle ordering avoids this only if Step 5/6 validation
  rejects blank supplierId.
     - Fix: make sure the validator rejects blank supplierId, and test it in
  Step 5/6. Alternatively, use `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` plus accept
  any string.
  2. **Step 6 RetryAfter header.**
     - `RetryAfter` is a sub-second TimeSpan. The header needs whole seconds
  rounded up and clamped to at least 1: `(int)Math.Ceiling(ra.TotalSeconds)`.
     - Plan line 151 already says "rounded up". Put this in one small helper and
  unit test it: `1ms` gives 1, `60s` gives 60, `60.0001s` gives 61.
  3. **ValidateOnStart is not covered by any automated test.**
     - The service-collection tests resolve `IOptions.Value`, which would still
  pass if `ValidateOnStart()` were deleted. The plan says it was verified by
  manual runs only.
     - Fix: add a test that builds a `Host` with a bad config and asserts
  `StartAsync` throws `OptionsValidationException`, or do it in a Step 7
  `WebApplicationFactory` test.

  **Nits / observations**
  4. **WebApplicationFactory and the singleton (Step 7).**
     - A shared factory (OneTimeSetUp) shares one limiter across tests. The
  101-request test must use a unique supplierId or a fresh factory.
     - `TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System)` (extensions.cs:16) is overridable
  via `ConfigureTestServices(s => s.AddSingleton<TimeProvider>(fake))`, because
  the last registration wins. A `FakeTimeProvider` also replaces the clock for
  any other TimeProvider consumer, such as Step 5 timestamps. Its default start
  is 2000-01-01, so it is not "now".
     - Options are read once in the limiter constructor (:22-23). Config
  overrides must therefore be applied through factory configuration before the
  host builds, not changed afterwards. That is fine, but note it.
  5. **RateLimitResult.cs:6-10.**
     - `default(RateLimitResult)` means rejected with zero RetryAfter.
     - The public constructor allows inconsistent combinations such as `(true,
  5s)`.
     - `Permit` is a property while `Reject` is a method, which is slightly
  inconsistent.
     - Acceptable as is. Optionally make the constructor private/internal so
  only `Permit`/`Reject` create values.
  6. **XML docs.**
     - `RateLimitOptions.cs:8,10,14` (properties and `SectionName`) and
  `RateLimitingServiceCollectionExtensions` (class and method) have no
  `<summary>`. The existing comments are accurate.
     - The IRateLimiter doc "permitted again as soon as its oldest counted
  request leaves the window" is accurate.
  7. **Plan staleness.**
     - Plan line 109 says "113 tests passing", but the suite now has 118. I am
  uncertain whether the extra 5 come from later work.
     - Plan line 112 names `ConcurrentDictionary<string, Window>`, but the code
  type is `WindowLog` (SlidingWindowRateLimiter.cs:35).
     - Plan line 113 says "dequeue timestamps `<= now - 60s`". That is
  equivalent to the code, but the code is written in terms of elapsed time.
     - CLAUDE.md line 39 matches the code.
  8. **Duplicate computation (:48, :56).** `GetElapsedTime` for the peeked item
  is computed twice, so cache it in a local if desired. This is trivial.
  9. **Unbounded growth.** Idle ids are never evicted, which is accepted. In
  Step 5, supplierIds from unvalidated requests would create dictionary entries,
  so validate first (the plan already orders it that way).

  ## Test quality (SlidingWindowRateLimiterTests.cs and the others)
  - **Meaningful behavior.** The tests assert real behavior: the 100/101 split
  with RetryAfter = 60s, rolling expiry with 50+50, straddle-boundary
  non-doubling, and rejected-does-not-extend. They are not vacuous. Each
  assertion distinguishes the mutations the author reports (counting rejected
  requests, off-by-one).
  - **Concurrency.** The concurrency tests (:181-213) assert exactly 100
  permitted, exactly 200 rejected, positive RetryAfter, and per-id exactness
  across 10 ids. Removing the lock would very likely turn them red, because
  `Queue` is unsafe and check-then-act races over-permit. They are
  probabilistic, though, and a frozen `FakeTimeProvider` cannot detect an
  ordering bug from reading the clock outside the lock.
  - **Gaps (minor).**

     Reservations Ingest API: Implementation Plan

     Context

     Mize home assignment: an ASP.NET Core (.NET 8) Web API on SQLite with
     Dapper (required by the assignment) that sits in front of a reservations
     table and handles two problems: duplicate supplier updates and over-eager
     suppliers.

     - POST /api/reservations/ingest: save, dedup, update, and throttle at more
       than 100 requests per rolling 60s per supplier.
     - GET /api/reservations/stats/{supplierId}: ingested vs throttled counts.

     The repo is a blank webapi template (ReservationsHandler.Api, net8.0,
     Swagger, weather sample in Program.cs). There are no Dapper, SQLite or test
     projects yet.

     Scope: 2-3 days, so a clean structure, sound concurrency, and focused
     tests. No auth, observability or migrations tooling.

     The assignment grades the Claude Code process as well as the code: the
     transcript, pushback and tradeoff judgment. Each step below is a natural
     prompt-sized unit. See "Working with Claude Code" at the end.

     Decisions (confirmed with you)

     ┌───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │     Topic     │                        Decision                         │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Stale updates │ If updatedAtUtc is older than the stored one, do not    │
     │               │ write. Return a Stale outcome.                          │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Throttle      │ Only accepted requests fill the window, so it clears    │
     │ counting      │ after 60s. Rejected ones don't extend it.               │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │               │ In-memory, thread-safe, sliding-window log per          │
     │ Limiter       │ supplier. README notes that production needs external   │
     │ storage       │ storage (e.g. Redis) for restarts and multiple          │
     │               │ instances.                                              │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │               │ ingested = created + updated. Duplicates and stale      │
     │ Stats         │ updates are not counted. Unknown supplier returns       │
     │               │ {ingested:0, throttled:0}.                              │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │               │ 201 Created (no Location header), 200 Updated, 200      │
     │ Responses     │ Duplicate, 200 Stale. Every success body has an         │
     │               │ explicit status. 429 + Retry-After for throttled. 400   │
     │               │ ProblemDetails for invalid input.                       │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Test          │ NUnit                                                   │
     │ framework     │                                                         │
     ├───────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │ Reservation   │ Composite (supplierId, reservationId), see below.       │
     │ identity      │                                                         │
     └───────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

     Why the composite key

     The spec's "same reservationId" could be read as reservationId alone. But
     ids are issued by each supplier independently, so collisions across
     suppliers are realistic. Keying on reservationId alone would let supplier B
     silently overwrite supplier A's record and muddy per-supplier stats. A
     reservation is therefore identified by who sent it plus their id. The
     alternative (global key plus a 409 when the supplier differs) was rejected
     as extra rules the spec never asked for. This goes in the README.

     My assumptions (to list in the README)

     - Identity is (supplierId, reservationId). Different suppliers may reuse
       the same reservation id, and cannot update each other's records.
     - "Same details" means roomId, checkIn, checkOut, price and updatedAtUtc
       are all equal. Equal updatedAtUtc with other fields different is treated
       as an Update (the spec says different details means update).
     - Order of checks is validate, then throttle, then ingest.
       - Throttle must precede all DB access, since its purpose is to protect
         the DB.
       - Validate must precede throttle because the limiter keys on supplierId,
         which an invalid body may not have.
       - Tradeoff: a supplier flooding invalid requests is not throttled. Those
         requests are cheap (no DB, no state), so this is accepted and
         documented.
     - Supplier ids are matched exactly (case-sensitive, trimmed).
     - Validation rules: required non-empty strings, checkOut strictly after 
       checkIn (equal values are rejected), price >= 0.

     Target structure

     Single API project with folders (a four-project Clean Architecture would be
     over-engineering here), plus one test project.

     README.md

     Testing rule (applies to every step)

     Every step ends with a "Unit tests" sub-step covering the code that step
     generated, written before moving on. If a step produced nothing
     unit-testable (Step 1), it says so and writes none. A step is only done
     when dotnet build and dotnet test are green.

     - Unit tests are fast, need no DB or HTTP, and use hand-written fakes (no
       mocking library) and FakeTimeProvider. They live in the test project in
       folders that mirror the source folders (Domain/, Contracts/,
       RateLimiting/, Services/, Controllers/, Data/).
     - Integration tests (real SQLite temp file, WebApplicationFactory) are all
       kept in Step 7. Anything that needs the database or full HTTP pipeline
       waits until then, even when it belongs to an earlier step's code
       (repository SQL, initializer, round trips, end-to-end status codes).
     - NUnit conventions: [TestFixture], [SetUp]/[TearDown], [TestCase] for
       variants, Assert.That(..., Is...). Don't mark fixtures that share state
       as [Parallelizable].

     Step-by-step

     Step 1. Scaffold and packages

     - Delete the weather sample from Program.cs. Keep Swagger in Development.
     - Add packages: Dapper, Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.
     - Create the NUnit test project (dotnet new nunit) with NUnit,
       NUnit3TestAdapter, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk,
       Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing,
       Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing. Reference the API project and
       add it to the .sln.
     - Add public partial class Program; so WebApplicationFactory can see it.
     - Why: a clean baseline before any logic. TimeProvider.Testing lets us test
       the 60s window without sleeping.
     - Unit tests: none, since there is no logic yet. (Done.)

     Step 2. Domain and contracts

     - Reservation as an immutable record (SupplierId, ReservationId, RoomId,
       CheckIn, CheckOut, Price (decimal), UpdatedAtUtc, plus a
       SameDetailsAs(other) method).
     - IngestStatus { Created, Updated, Duplicate, Stale, Throttled }.
     - Request DTO with DataAnnotations plus IValidatableObject for checkOut > 
       checkIn. [ApiController] then gives automatic 400 ProblemDetails.
     - Use DateTimeOffset and normalize to UTC at the boundary. Use decimal for
       money.
     - Why: keeps the HTTP contract separate from the domain and avoids a
       validation library for 4 rules.
     - Code is already written. Unit tests still to write (backfill, do next):
       - Reservation.SameDetailsAs: identical gives true. Each single field
         differing (room, checkIn, checkOut, price, updatedAtUtc) gives false,
         as a [TestCase] per field. Same instant in different offsets is equal.
         450.00m equals 450.0m. Identity fields (supplier/reservation id) are
         ignored.
       - IngestReservationRequest validation, via
         Validator.TryValidateObject(..., validateAllProperties: true): valid
         request passes. Each missing field fails. Empty and whitespace strings
         fail. checkOut == checkIn and checkOut < checkIn fail. checkOut one
         tick after checkIn passes. Negative price fails, price 0 passes.
       - ToReservation(): ids trimmed, non-UTC offsets normalized to UTC.
       - Whether MVC still reports the cross-field error alongside property
         errors is an HTTP-pipeline behavior, so it is verified in Step 7.

     Step 3. Data layer (Dapper and SQLite)

     - IDbConnectionFactory.OpenConnectionAsync() returns an open DbConnection.
       SqliteConnectionFactory is built by a lazy DI factory that reads
       ConnectionStrings:Reservations from the final IConfiguration (Data 
       Source=reservations.db), so tests can override it with a temp file.
     - DatabaseInitializer runs CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS at startup:
       - Reservations(SupplierId, ReservationId, RoomId, CheckIn, CheckOut, 
         Price, UpdatedAtUtc, PRIMARY KEY (SupplierId, ReservationId))
       - SupplierStats(SupplierId PRIMARY KEY, Ingested INTEGER, Throttled 
         INTEGER)
     - Type handlers (kept, with a required workaround for dates):
       DateTimeOffsetTypeHandler (fixed-width ISO-8601 UTC text, sortable) is
       needed for reading and writing. A scratch test showed that Dapper does
       NOT call a handler's SetValue for built-in types unless the built-in
       mapping is removed first, so DapperConfiguration.RegisterTypeHandlers()
       calls SqlMapper.RemoveTypeMap for DateTimeOffset (and its nullable)
       before AddTypeHandler. DecimalTypeHandler is read-only: experiments
       showed that without it Dapper cannot map the TEXT Price column into the
       record's decimal parameter (all cases failed), but that
       Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's native decimal write is already invariant text
       that round-trips exactly (checked under de-DE, including decimal.MaxValue
       and 28-digit fractions), so no RemoveTypeMap or custom write is needed
       for decimal. Registration is process-wide and runs once. Dapper then maps
       rows straight into the Reservation and SupplierStats records (SELECT
       column order must match the constructor parameter order).
     - Connection abstraction: IDbConnectionFactory.OpenConnectionAsync()
       returns a System.Data.Common.DbConnection. Repositories depend only on
       that and on IsolationLevel.Serializable for the write lock (SQLite maps
       it to BEGIN IMMEDIATE). Only SqliteConnectionFactory references
       Microsoft.Data.Sqlite. The SQL text itself (ON CONFLICT, WITHOUT ROWID)
       is still SQLite-flavored.
     - The pure dedup decision is the static Reservation.Evaluate(existing, 
       incoming) (Created, Duplicate, Stale, Updated), next to SameDetailsAs, so
       it is unit-testable without a DB. The repository only performs the write
       the status implies.
     - IReservationRepository.UpsertAsync(reservation) runs in one write 
       transaction:
       a. SELECT the existing row by key.
       b. None: INSERT, giving Created.
       c. Identical: nothing is written, giving Duplicate.
       d. Incoming updatedAtUtc is older: nothing is written, giving Stale.
       e. Otherwise UPDATE, giving Updated.
       f. For Created and Updated, increment SupplierStats.Ingested in the same
          transaction (atomic upsert: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET 
          Ingested = Ingested + 1).
     - ISupplierStatsRepository: IncrementThrottledAsync, GetAsync (zeros if no
       row).
     - Concurrency: the SELECT-then-write must not race (two identical
       concurrent requests must yield exactly one Created). Use an immediate
       (write-locking) transaction. Confirm that Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's chosen 
       isolation level really takes the write lock up front, and prove it with 
       the concurrency test in Step 7. If it doesn't, fall back to a per-key
       SemaphoreSlim.
     - No explicit PRAGMA busy_timeout is needed: Microsoft.Data.Sqlite applies
       its Default Timeout (30s) as the busy timeout when a connection opens, so
       concurrent writers wait instead of throwing "database is locked".
     - Unit tests (done, 84 total passing): DapperConfigurationTests proves the
       Dapper setup on a single in-memory connection with its own minimal table
       (date write format, nullable dates, price stored as text, record round
       trip incl. a Duplicate check, prices under de-DE, double registration
       harmless); it was verified to fail 11 of 12 when the RemoveTypeMap
       workaround is removed. Reservation.Evaluate (all outcomes, including
       equal updatedAtUtc and offset-insensitivity). DateTimeOffsetTypeHandler
       (UTC normalization, tick precision, culture invariance with th-TH, round
       trip, chronological text sorting across offsets, malformed text and
       non-text values throw) and DecimalTypeHandler (read-only: exact parsing
       of stored text incl. extremes, culture invariance with de-DE, no float
       drift, malformed text and non-text values throw). SqliteConnectionFactory
       (rejects blank connection strings, returns a fresh open connection each
       time, fails cleanly on an unopenable database; uses Data Source=:memory:
       so no file is needed). The repositories, initializer and real round trips
       need SQLite, so they are integration tests in Step 7.
     - Verified with a throwaway scratch test (deleted; recreate properly in 
       Step 7): text storage format, round trip, 20 parallel identical upserts
       give exactly 1 Created and 19 Duplicate with ingested == 1, 10 parallel
       throttled increments give 10. With a weaker isolation level
       (ReadUncommitted, or earlier deferred: true) the concurrency test fails
       with SQLite Error 5: 'database is locked', so it genuinely proves
       IsolationLevel.Serializable (BEGIN IMMEDIATE) is what makes it safe.

     Step 4. Rate limiter (the interesting part)

     - IRateLimiter.TryAcquire(id) -> RateLimitResult(Permitted, RetryAfter).
       (Step 4 done; the full suite is green.)
     - Built beyond the original sketch: validation attributes on
       RateLimitOptions ([Range(1, int.MaxValue)] on the limit;
       [Range(typeof(TimeSpan), ...)] from one tick to a one-day sanity cap on
       the window) with ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart(), so a bad
       config stops the app at startup (covered by
       RateLimitingStartupValidationTests, which start a real host and fail if
       ValidateOnStart() is removed; also verified by real runs with
       PermitLimit=0 and Window=00:00:00; also verified culture-independent
       under de-DE, fr-FR, th-TH), AddRateLimiting() extension (binds the
       RateLimiting config section, TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System),
       singleton limiter), and RateLimiting defaults in appsettings.json.
     - The log stores monotonic TimeProvider.GetTimestamp() values
       (Queue<long>), not wall-clock DateTimeOffset, so clock adjustments cannot
       shorten or stretch the window. The clock is read inside the per-id lock
       so the queue stays chronological under contention. A request exactly one
       window old counts as expired.
     - SlidingWindowRateLimiter implements the sliding window log algorithm
       (singleton): one log of accepted-request timestamps per id (the app uses
       the supplierId as the id). ConcurrentDictionary<string, WindowLog>, where
       each WindowLog holds a Queue<long> of monotonic timestamps (the log, in
       chronological order) guarded by a private _lock object.
       - On each call (inside the lock): read the clock, then dequeue timestamps
         whose elapsed time is >= window. If count >= limit, reject with
         RetryAfter = window - elapsed(oldest), which is always strictly
         positive. Otherwise enqueue now and allow.
       - Rejected calls enqueue nothing (per your decision).
     - RateLimitOptions (limit = 100, window = 60s) bound via IOptions, so tests
       can use small values if needed.
     - Inject TimeProvider (built into .NET 8) instead of calling
       DateTime.UtcNow.
     - Why a sliding log over a fixed window: the spec says "any rolling
       60-second window". A fixed window allows 200 requests across a boundary.
       Memory is bounded at 100 timestamps per supplier.
     - Known limitation (README): in-memory state is lost on restart and not
       shared across instances. Idle windows are never evicted, which is fine at
       this scale.
     - Unit tests (done; FakeTimeProvider, no DB). Verified by deliberately 
       breaking the code: counting rejected requests, an off-by-one at the 
       boundary, and removing the lock each turn the suite red.
       - 100 calls allowed, 101st rejected with a sensible RetryAfter.
       - After advancing 60s the supplier is allowed again, and the window is
         truly rolling (requests at t=0 and t=30 expire independently).
       - Boundary: a timestamp exactly 60s old has expired.
       - Suppliers are isolated from each other.
       - Rejected calls don't extend the window.
       - Small custom RateLimitOptions are honored.
       - Concurrency: 300 parallel calls produce exactly 100 allowed.

     Step 5. Ingestion service

     IReservationIngestionService.IngestAsync(Reservation) orchestrates:
     1. limiter.TryAcquire(supplierId). If denied,
        stats.IncrementThrottledAsync, then return Throttled(retryAfter).
     2. Otherwise reservationRepo.UpsertAsync and return the outcome.

     It returns a small result type (status plus optional RetryAfter), not
     exceptions. Exceptions are for exceptional cases only. Why this layer: the
     controller stays trivial and the logic is unit-testable with fakes.
     - Unit tests (hand-written fake limiter and fake repositories):
       - Limiter allows, so the repository is called and its outcome is returned
         unchanged (Created, Updated, Duplicate, Stale).
       - Limiter denies, so the result is Throttled with the RetryAfter, the
         throttled counter is incremented exactly once, and the repository is
         never called.
       - The limiter is asked with the reservation's supplierId.
       - The cancellation token is passed through.
       - A repository exception propagates (not swallowed).

     Step 6. Controller and error handling

     - POST /api/reservations/ingest maps the outcome:
       - Created: 201 with a body and no Location header (use StatusCode(201, 
         body), not CreatedAtAction).
       - Updated, Duplicate, Stale: 200.
       - Throttled: 429 with a Retry-After header and ProblemDetails.
       - Body: { status, supplierId, reservationId }.
     - GET /api/reservations/stats/{supplierId} returns { supplierId, ingested, 
       throttled }.
     - GlobalExceptionHandler (IExceptionHandler, .NET 8) turns unexpected
       errors into a 500 ProblemDetails with no stack trace leaked. Log the
       exception.
     - Register everything in Program.cs through small AddXxx extension methods.
       Add CancellationToken through the stack.
     - Unit tests (controller called directly with a fake service, no HTTP):
       - Each status maps to the right result: Created gives 201 with the body
         and no Location header. Updated, Duplicate and Stale give 200 with the
         matching status. Throttled gives 429 with a Retry-After header (whole
         seconds, rounded up) and ProblemDetails.
       - The request is mapped to the domain Reservation (normalized) before the
         service is called.
       - Stats endpoint returns the counts from a fake stats repository, and
         zeros pass through.
       - GlobalExceptionHandler: an unexpected exception yields a 500
         ProblemDetails with no stack trace or message leaked, and the exception
         is logged.
       - Full end-to-end HTTP behavior is covered in Step 7.

     Step 7. Integration tests (the grader's confidence signal)

     Only integration tests are written here. All unit tests were written in
     their own steps. Each test class gets a fresh temp-file SQLite DB via
     WebApplicationFactory ([SetUp]/[TearDown]). Concurrency tests use
     Task.WhenAll. Don't mark these fixtures [Parallelizable].

     Integration (WebApplicationFactory with a temp-file SQLite DB per test 
     class):
     - Repository and initializer against real SQLite: schema is created
       idempotently, one row per (supplierId, reservationId), and SupplierStats
       counters are atomic.
     - Created (201), then identical resend (200 Duplicate, with proof no write 
       happened, e.g. ingested stat unchanged and the row unchanged), then
       changed price (200 Updated, row updated), then older updatedAtUtc (Stale,
       row unchanged).
     - Same reservationId from two different suppliers gives two independent
       rows (one can't overwrite the other).
     - Concurrency: N parallel identical ingests produce exactly 1 Created, N-1
       Duplicate, and ingested == 1.
     - 101st request from a supplier gets 429 with Retry-After. Another supplier
       is unaffected. Stats show ingested=100, throttled=1.
     - Validation over real HTTP: missing fields, checkOut == checkIn, checkOut 
       < checkIn and negative price each return 400 ProblemDetails. checkOut one
       tick after checkIn is accepted. Also confirm the checkOut error is
       reported when other fields are invalid too (see Step 2 note).
     - An unexpected failure returns 500 ProblemDetails over HTTP.
     - 201 response has no Location header.
     - Stats for an unknown supplier return zeros.
     - Decimal and date round-trip fidelity through SQLite.

     Step 8. README (half a page, as the assignment requires)

     Three sections:
     1. Assumptions: the list above, with reasons.
     2. Claude suggestions I disagreed with or changed: fill this in honestly
        during the session.
     3. With more time: distributed limiter (Redis), migrations
        (DbUp/FluentMigrator), idempotency/outbox, auth, metrics, eviction of
        idle limiter windows, a store that scales beyond SQLite's single writer.

     Also note how to run and test: dotnet run, dotnet test.

     Deliberately out of scope

     - Auth, observability, migrations tooling, Docker.
     - MediatR, CQRS, repository generics, AutoMapper, FluentValidation: they
       add ceremony with no payoff at this size.
     - GET-by-id endpoint (not in the spec).

     Verification

     1. dotnet build and dotnet test are green after every step (unit tests per
        step, integration tests from Step 7).
     2. dotnet run, then via Swagger or the .http file:
        - POST a reservation: 201 Created.
        - POST it again: 200 Duplicate.
        - Change the price and POST: 200 Updated.
        - POST with an older updatedAtUtc: 200 Stale.
        - Loop 101 POSTs for one supplier: the 101st returns 429 with
          Retry-After.
        - GET /api/reservations/stats/{supplierId} returns the expected counts.
     3. Inspect reservations.db (e.g. sqlite3) to confirm there is one row per
        key and the stats counters match.
     4. Add *.db to .gitignore.

● Step 5, the ingestion service, is done and I stopped before Step 6. A full
  rebuild gives 0 warnings and 0 errors, and all 149 tests pass (124 before, 25
  new). I didn't touch git.

  What was built (Services/)
  - IReservationIngestionService: IngestAsync(Reservation, CancellationToken)
    returns an IngestResult.
  - ReservationIngestionService: it asks the limiter about the reservation's
    supplierId.
    - Rejected: it increments the supplier's throttled counter and returns
      Throttled(retryAfter). The reservations table is never touched.
    - Permitted: it calls UpsertAsync and returns that outcome unchanged:
      Created, Updated, Duplicate or Stale.
  - IngestResult:
    - An expected outcome like throttling is a result, not an exception.
    - Only the throttled result carries a RetryAfter.
    - Two factories make misuse hard: Processed(status) rejects Throttled, and
      Throttled(retryAfter) requires the wait.
  - AddIngestion(): registers the service as a singleton and is called from
    Program.cs.

  Tests
  - Hand-written fakes: in Fakes/, with an ordered call log. They're reusable
    for the Step 6 controller tests.
  - Service behavior:
    - All four repository outcomes pass through unchanged.
    - A throttled request is counted exactly once and never reaches the
      repository.
    - The limiter is asked with the supplier id, and runs before any database
      work.
    - Cancellation tokens are passed through.
    - Repository and stats failures propagate.
    - A null reservation is rejected before any collaborator is called.
  - Two composition tests with the real limiter and a fake clock:
    - With a limit of 3, exactly 3 requests reach the repository and 2 are
      throttled, each counted once with a 10-second RetryAfter.
    - A throttled supplier doesn't affect another one, and recovers after the
      window.
  - The tests can fail. I deliberately broke the service three ways, and each
    turned the suite red. The bugs were writing to the database when throttled
    (3 failures), not counting a throttled request (6) and limiting by
    reservationId instead of supplierId (3). I restored the code and confirmed
    nothing was left behind.
  - Startup: I started the app in Development, which validates the whole
    dependency graph. It started with no errors in the log.

  Two decisions for the README, recorded in the plan
  1. If the stats write fails while throttling, the error propagates and returns
     a 500 instead of being swallowed. A supplier that should get a 429 would
     then get a 500 when the stats table is unavailable. I chose honesty over
     hiding a lost counter. The alternative is to log the failure and still
     return the 429, and I can switch if you prefer.
  2. A request that consumed a limiter slot still counts against the supplier
     even if the later database write fails.

  I also fixed an analyzer warning in my own equality test, which had two
  identical expressions on both sides of an assertion.

  Say "go" for Step 6, the controller and error handling. As agreed, its tests
  will include the whole-seconds Retry-After helper and a check that blank
  supplier ids never reach the limiter.

> isnt IngestionServiceCollectionExtensions redundemt? or is it still worth a   
  class and func to keep conventions?                                           

● It's redundant today. It's one line wrapped in a class, a method and a using,
  and it has its own two-test file. I wouldn't add it again.

  Where the extension-method convention earns its place
  - AddDataAccess() hides a lazy lambda that reads the connection string, the
    Dapper handler registration, and three registrations.
  - AddRateLimiting() hides options binding, validation, ValidateOnStart, the
    TimeProvider default and the singleton choice.
  - In both, the details belong next to the code they configure, and Program.cs
    stays readable.

  Why AddIngestion() doesn't meet that bar
  It only does services.AddSingleton<IReservationIngestionService, 
  ReservationIngestionService>(). That line is as readable in Program.cs as the
  call to hide it, so the wrapper only adds indirection and a file to open. The
  singleton rationale fits in a one-line comment. My plan said "register
  everything through small AddXxx extension methods", and I applied that rule
  mechanically here. It's a convention for non-trivial wiring, not a rule for
  every registration.

  The case for keeping it
  - Consistency: every feature gets one AddX() call in Program.cs.
  - A place to grow: if the service gains dependencies or options later, there's
    already a home for them.

  Both are weak. The first is a style preference. The second is speculative
  generality, and moving a line into a class later takes a minute.

  What removing it would involve
  - Put builder.Services.AddSingleton<IReservationIngestionService, 
    ReservationIngestionService>(); in Program.cs, with a short comment about
    why it's safe as a singleton.
  - Delete IngestionServiceCollectionExtensions.cs and its test file. The two
    tests there check little that isn't already covered. Running the app in
    Development validates the dependency graph at build time, and the Step 7
    integration tests will resolve the service through the real host.
  - Remove the using in Program.cs if nothing else needs it, and update the plan
    and CLAUDE.md.

  My recommendation is to remove it. I haven't changed anything, and I haven't
  started Step 6. Tell me to remove it, or to keep it, and say "go" when you're
  ready for Step 6.

● I recommend against a SupplierStatsService. It would be the clean,
  professional choice only if it contained logic, and it wouldn't.

  Why a pass-through service is the weaker choice
  - It would only forward a call. The stats endpoint reads two counters, and the
    repository already returns zeros for an unknown supplier. Anything a
    service would do is either already done or an HTTP concern.
  - It costs more than it looks. A pass-through needs an interface, a class, a
    DI registration, a fake and tests, and those tests only check that it
    forwards the call. That is code to read and maintain with no behavior behind
    it.
  - "Keeping order" is a weak reason. The POST goes through a service because it
    has real orchestration: throttle first, count the rejection, then write.
    The GET has nothing to orchestrate. Making the two look alike gives you a
    shallow layer. This is the usual complaint about ceremonial services, and
    reviewers notice it.
  - It's cheap to add later. If logic appears, such as derived values, caching
    or authorization, extracting a service is a small refactor, because the
    repository already sits behind an interface.

  What I'd do instead
  - The stats endpoint in the controller injects ISupplierStatsRepository
    directly.
  - The controller keeps the HTTP-level concerns: it trims the route supplierId
    and returns a 400 for a blank one. That also fixes the 500-on-blank-id
    finding from the review, since the repository throws on blank ids. It then
    maps the domain SupplierStats to SupplierStatsResponse, which stays a
    separate type as you decided earlier.
  - The cost to record in the README is a slight asymmetry: the controller
    depends on one service and one repository. The reason is that only one of
    the two endpoints has logic to orchestrate.

  I've written this into Step 6 of the plan. That covers the decision, the
  blank-id handling, the extra stats tests, and a line under "Deliberately out
  of scope". I haven't changed any code. If you'd still prefer the service for
  consistency, say so and I'll reverse that line of the plan.

     │ Why the composite key                                                   │
     │                                                                         │
     │ The spec's "same reservationId" could be read as reservationId alone.   │
     │ But ids are issued by each supplier independently, so collisions across │
     │ suppliers are realistic. Keying on reservationId alone would let        │
     │ supplier B silently overwrite supplier A's record and muddy             │
     │ per-supplier stats. A reservation is therefore identified by who sent   │
     │ it plus their id. The alternative (global key plus a 409 when the       │
     │ supplier differs) was rejected as extra rules the spec never asked for. │
     │ This goes in the README.                                                │
     │                                                                         │
     │ My assumptions (to list in the README)                                  │
     │                                                                         │
     │ - Identity is (supplierId, reservationId). Different suppliers may      │
     │   reuse the same reservation id, and cannot update each other's         │
     │   records.                                                              │
     │ - "Same details" means roomId, checkIn, checkOut, price and             │
     │   updatedAtUtc are all equal. Equal updatedAtUtc with other fields      │
     │   different is treated as an Update (the spec says different details    │
     │   means update).                                                        │
     │ - Order of checks is validate, then throttle, then ingest.              │
     │   - Throttle must precede all DB access, since its purpose is to        │
     │     protect the DB.                                                     │
     │   - Validate must precede throttle because the limiter keys on          │
     │     supplierId, which an invalid body may not have.                     │
     │   - Tradeoff: a supplier flooding invalid requests is not throttled.    │
     │     Those requests are cheap (no DB, no state), so this is accepted and │
     │     documented.                                                         │
     │ - Supplier ids are matched exactly (case-sensitive, trimmed).           │
     │ - Validation rules: required non-empty strings, checkOut strictly after │
     │   checkIn (equal values are rejected), price >= 0.                      │
     │                                                                         │
     │ Target structure                                                        │
     │                                                                         │
     │ Single API project with folders (a four-project Clean Architecture      │
     │ would be over-engineering here), plus one test project.                 │
     │                                                                         │
     │ ReservationsHandler.sln                                                 │
     │ ReservationsHandler.Api/                                                │
     │   Program.cs                      composition root only (extension      │
     │ methods for DI)                                                         │
     │   Controllers/ReservationsController.cs   thin: maps outcome -> HTTP    │
     │   Contracts/                      IngestReservationRequest,             │
     │ IngestReservationResponse, SupplierStatsResponse                        │
     │   Domain/                         Reservation (record), IngestStatus    │
     │ enum                                                                    │
     │   Services/                       IReservationIngestionService + impl   │
     │ (orchestration)                                                         │
     │   RateLimiting/                   IRateLimiter,                         │
     │ SlidingWindowRateLimiter, RateLimitOptions                              │
     │   Data/                           IDbConnectionFactory (+               │

     │ Testing rule (applies to every step)                                    │
     │                                                                         │
     │ Every step ends with a "Unit tests" sub-step covering the code that     │
     │ step generated, written before moving on. If a step produced nothing    │
     │ unit-testable (Step 1), it says so and writes none. A step is only done │

     │                                                                         │
     │ - Unit tests are fast, need no DB or HTTP, and use hand-written fakes   │
     │   (no mocking library) and FakeTimeProvider. They live in the test      │
     │   project in folders that mirror the source folders (Domain/,           │
     │   Contracts/, RateLimiting/, Services/, Controllers/, Data/).           │
     │ - Integration tests (real SQLite temp file, WebApplicationFactory) are  │
     │   all kept in Step 7. Anything that needs the database or full HTTP     │
     │   pipeline waits until then, even when it belongs to an earlier step's  │
     │   code (repository SQL, initializer, round trips, end-to-end status     │
     │   codes).                                                               │
     │ - NUnit conventions: [TestFixture], [SetUp]/[TearDown], [TestCase] for  │
     │   variants, Assert.That(..., Is...). Don't mark fixtures that share     │
     │   state as [Parallelizable].                                            │

     │ - Unit tests: none, since there is no logic yet. (Done.)                │
     │                                                                         │
     │ Step 2. Domain and contracts                                            │
     │                                                                         │
     │ - Reservation as an immutable record (SupplierId, ReservationId,        │
     │   RoomId, CheckIn, CheckOut, Price (decimal), UpdatedAtUtc, plus a      │
     │   SameDetailsAs(other) method).                                         │
     │ - IngestStatus { Created, Updated, Duplicate, Stale, Throttled }.       │
     │ - Request DTO with DataAnnotations plus IValidatableObject for checkOut │
     │   > checkIn. [ApiController] then gives automatic 400 ProblemDetails.   │
     │ - Use DateTimeOffset and normalize to UTC at the boundary. Use decimal  │
     │   for money.                                                            │
     │ - Why: keeps the HTTP contract separate from the domain and avoids a    │
     │   validation library for 4 rules.                                       │
     │ - Code is already written. Unit tests still to write (backfill, do      │
     │   next):                                                                │
     │   - Reservation.SameDetailsAs: identical gives true. Each single field  │
     │     differing (room, checkIn, checkOut, price, updatedAtUtc) gives      │
     │     false, as a [TestCase] per field. Same instant in different offsets │
     │     is equal. 450.00m equals 450.0m. Identity fields                    │
     │     (supplier/reservation id) are ignored.                              │
     │   - IngestReservationRequest validation, via                            │
     │     Validator.TryValidateObject(..., validateAllProperties: true):      │
     │     valid request passes. Each missing field fails. Empty and           │
     │     whitespace strings fail. checkOut == checkIn and checkOut < checkIn │
     │     fail. checkOut one tick after checkIn passes. Negative price        │
     │     fails, price 0 passes.                                              │
     │   - ToReservation(): ids trimmed, non-UTC offsets normalized to UTC.    │
     │   - Whether MVC still reports the cross-field error alongside property  │
     │     errors is an HTTP-pipeline behavior, so it is verified in Step 7.   │
     │                                                                         │
     │ Step 3. Data layer (Dapper and SQLite)                                  │
     │                                                                         │
     │ - IDbConnectionFactory.OpenConnectionAsync() returns an open            │
     │   DbConnection. SqliteConnectionFactory is built by a lazy DI factory   │
     │   that reads ConnectionStrings:Reservations from the final              │
     │   IConfiguration (Data Source=reservations.db), so tests can override   │
     │   it with a temp file.                                                  │
     │ - DatabaseInitializer runs CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS at startup:       │
     │   - Reservations(SupplierId, ReservationId, RoomId, CheckIn, CheckOut,  │
     │     Price, UpdatedAtUtc, PRIMARY KEY (SupplierId, ReservationId))       │
     │   - SupplierStats(SupplierId PRIMARY KEY, Ingested INTEGER, Throttled   │
     │     INTEGER)                                                            │
     │ - Type handlers (kept, with a required workaround for dates):           │
     │   DateTimeOffsetTypeHandler (fixed-width ISO-8601 UTC text, sortable)   │
     │   is needed for reading and writing. A scratch test showed that Dapper  │
     │   does NOT call a handler's SetValue for built-in types unless the      │
     │   built-in mapping is removed first, so                                 │
     │   DapperConfiguration.RegisterTypeHandlers() calls                      │
     │   SqlMapper.RemoveTypeMap for DateTimeOffset (and its nullable) before  │
     │   AddTypeHandler. DecimalTypeHandler is read-only: experiments showed   │
     │   that without it Dapper cannot map the TEXT Price column into the      │
     │   record's decimal parameter (all cases failed), but that               │
     │   Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's native decimal write is already invariant     │
     │   text that round-trips exactly (checked under de-DE, including         │
     │   decimal.MaxValue and 28-digit fractions), so no RemoveTypeMap or      │
     │   custom write is needed for decimal. Registration is process-wide and  │
     │   runs once. Dapper then maps rows straight into the Reservation and    │
     │   SupplierStats records (SELECT column order must match the constructor │
     │   parameter order).                                                     │
     │ - Connection abstraction: IDbConnectionFactory.OpenConnectionAsync()    │
     │   returns a System.Data.Common.DbConnection. Repositories depend only   │
     │   on that and on IsolationLevel.Serializable for the write lock (SQLite │
     │   maps it to BEGIN IMMEDIATE). Only SqliteConnectionFactory references  │
     │   Microsoft.Data.Sqlite. The SQL text itself (ON CONFLICT, WITHOUT      │
     │   ROWID) is still SQLite-flavored.                                      │
     │ - The pure dedup decision is the static Reservation.Evaluate(existing,  │
     │   incoming) (Created, Duplicate, Stale, Updated), next to               │
     │   SameDetailsAs, so it is unit-testable without a DB. The repository    │
     │   only performs the write the status implies.                           │
     │ - IReservationRepository.UpsertAsync(reservation) runs in one write     │
     │   transaction:                                                          │
     │   a. SELECT the existing row by key.                                    │
     │   b. None: INSERT, giving Created.                                      │
     │   c. Identical: nothing is written, giving Duplicate.                   │
     │   d. Incoming updatedAtUtc is older: nothing is written, giving Stale.  │
     │   e. Otherwise UPDATE, giving Updated.                                  │
     │   f. For Created and Updated, increment SupplierStats.Ingested in the   │
     │      same transaction (atomic upsert: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE  │
     │      SET Ingested = Ingested + 1).                                      │
     │ - ISupplierStatsRepository: IncrementThrottledAsync, GetAsync (zeros if │
     │   no row).                                                              │
     │ - Concurrency: the SELECT-then-write must not race (two identical       │
     │   concurrent requests must yield exactly one Created). Use an immediate │
     │   (write-locking) transaction. Confirm that Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's     │
     │   chosen isolation level really takes the write lock up front, and      │
     │   prove it with the concurrency test in Step 7. If it doesn't, fall     │
     │   back to a per-key SemaphoreSlim.                                      │
     │ - No explicit PRAGMA busy_timeout is needed: Microsoft.Data.Sqlite      │
     │   applies its Default Timeout (30s) as the busy timeout when a          │
     │   connection opens, so concurrent writers wait instead of throwing      │
     │   "database is locked".                                                 │
     │ - Unit tests (done, 84 total passing): DapperConfigurationTests proves  │
     │   the Dapper setup on a single in-memory connection with its own        │
     │   minimal table (date write format, nullable dates, price stored as     │
     │   text, record round trip incl. a Duplicate check, prices under de-DE,  │
     │   double registration harmless); it was verified to fail 11 of 12 when  │
     │   the RemoveTypeMap workaround is removed. Reservation.Evaluate (all    │
     │   outcomes, including equal updatedAtUtc and offset-insensitivity).     │
     │   DateTimeOffsetTypeHandler (UTC normalization, tick precision, culture │
     │   invariance with th-TH, round trip, chronological text sorting across  │
     │   offsets, malformed text and non-text values throw) and                │
     │   DecimalTypeHandler (read-only: exact parsing of stored text incl.     │
     │   extremes, culture invariance with de-DE, no float drift, malformed    │
     │   text and non-text values throw). SqliteConnectionFactory (rejects     │
     │   blank connection strings, returns a fresh open connection each time,  │
     │   fails cleanly on an unopenable database; uses Data Source=:memory: so │
     │   no file is needed). The repositories, initializer and real round      │
     │   trips need SQLite, so they are integration tests in Step 7.           │
     │ - Verified with a throwaway scratch test (deleted; recreate properly in │
     │   Step 7): text storage format, round trip, 20 parallel identical       │
     │   upserts give exactly 1 Created and 19 Duplicate with ingested == 1,   │
     │   10 parallel throttled increments give 10. With a weaker isolation     │
     │   level (ReadUncommitted, or earlier deferred: true) the concurrency    │
     │   test fails with SQLite Error 5: 'database is locked', so it genuinely │
     │   proves IsolationLevel.Serializable (BEGIN IMMEDIATE) is what makes    │
     │   it safe.                                                              │
     │                                                                         │
     │ Step 4. Rate limiter (the interesting part)                             │
     │                                                                         │
     │ - IRateLimiter.TryAcquire(id) -> RateLimitResult(Permitted,             │
     │   RetryAfter). (Step 4 done; the full suite is green.)                  │
     │ - Built beyond the original sketch: validation attributes on            │
     │   RateLimitOptions ([Range(1, int.MaxValue)] on the limit;              │
     │   [Range(typeof(TimeSpan), ...)] from one tick to a one-day sanity cap  │
     │   on the window) with ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart(), so a │
     │   bad config stops the app at startup (covered by                       │
     │   RateLimitingStartupValidationTests, which start a real host and fail  │
     │   if ValidateOnStart() is removed; also verified by real runs with      │
     │   PermitLimit=0 and Window=00:00:00; also verified culture-independent  │
     │   under de-DE, fr-FR, th-TH), AddRateLimiting() extension (binds the    │
     │   RateLimiting config section, TryAddSingleton(TimeProvider.System),    │
     │   singleton limiter), and RateLimiting defaults in appsettings.json.    │
     │ - The log stores monotonic TimeProvider.GetTimestamp() values           │
     │   (Queue<long>), not wall-clock DateTimeOffset, so clock adjustments    │
     │   cannot shorten or stretch the window. The clock is read inside the    │
     │   per-id lock so the queue stays chronological under contention. A      │
     │   request exactly one window old counts as expired.                     │
     │ - SlidingWindowRateLimiter implements the sliding window log algorithm  │
     │   (singleton): one log of accepted-request timestamps per id (the app   │
     │   uses the supplierId as the id). ConcurrentDictionary<string,          │
     │   WindowLog>, where each WindowLog holds a Queue<long> of monotonic     │
     │   timestamps (the log, in chronological order) guarded by a private     │
     │   _lock object.                                                         │
     │   - On each call (inside the lock): read the clock, then dequeue        │
     │     timestamps whose elapsed time is >= window. If count >= limit,      │
     │     reject with RetryAfter = window - elapsed(oldest), which is always  │
     │     strictly positive. Otherwise enqueue now and allow.                 │
     │   - Rejected calls enqueue nothing (per your decision).                 │
     │ - RateLimitOptions (limit = 100, window = 60s) bound via IOptions, so   │
     │   tests can use small values if needed.                                 │
     │ - Inject TimeProvider (built into .NET 8) instead of calling            │
     │   DateTime.UtcNow.                                                      │
     │ - Why a sliding log over a fixed window: the spec says "any rolling     │
     │   60-second window". A fixed window allows 200 requests across a        │
     │   boundary. Memory is bounded at 100 timestamps per supplier.           │
     │ - Known limitation (README): in-memory state is lost on restart and not │
     │   shared across instances. Idle windows are never evicted, which is     │
     │   fine at this scale.                                                   │
     │ - Unit tests (done; FakeTimeProvider, no DB). Verified by deliberately  │
     │   breaking the code: counting rejected requests, an off-by-one at the   │
     │   boundary, and removing the lock each turn the suite red.              │
     │   - 100 calls allowed, 101st rejected with a sensible RetryAfter.       │
     │   - After advancing 60s the supplier is allowed again, and the window   │
     │     is truly rolling (requests at t=0 and t=30 expire independently).   │
     │   - Boundary: a timestamp exactly 60s old has expired.                  │
     │   - Suppliers are isolated from each other.                             │
     │   - Rejected calls don't extend the window.                             │
     │   - Small custom RateLimitOptions are honored.                          │
